clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene encoding bestrophin-1, a chloride channel in the retinal pigment epithelium
The hallmark early lesion is a round, yellow, yolk-like (vitelliform) deposit at the fovea, best appreciated on fundus examination
Progresses through recognised stages: previtelliform, vitelliform (egg-yolk), pseudohypopyon (layering of material), vitelliruptive (scrambled egg), and atrophic or fibrotic scarring
The electro-oculogram (EOG) is diagnostic and characteristically abnormal, with a markedly reduced Arden light-rise ratio even when the full-field electroretinogram (ERG) is normal
Optical coherence tomography shows subretinal accumulation of hyperreflective vitelliform material between the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium
Central vision is often preserved for years despite a striking macular appearance, and the condition may be found incidentally
Choroidal neovascularisation is an important sight-threatening complication that can be treated with anti-VEGF therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Best vitelliform macular dystrophy results from mutations in BEST1, which encodes bestrophin-1, a calcium-activated chloride channel located on the basolateral membrane of retinal pigment epithelial cells. Dysfunction of this channel disturbs ion and fluid transport across the retinal pigment epithelium and impairs the standing potential of the eye, which underlies the abnormal electro-oculogram. Lipofuscin-like material accumulates within and beneath the retinal pigment epithelium in the subretinal space at the macula, forming the characteristic vitelliform lesion. Over time this deposited material breaks down and disperses, leading to photoreceptor loss, geographic atrophy, and sometimes fibrous scarring, with the risk of secondary choroidal neovascularisation.
additionalDifferentials: Age-related macular degeneration with drusen or neovascular membrane
additionalInvestigations: Electro-oculography demonstrating a reduced Arden light-rise ratio
Full-field electroretinography, typically normal, to distinguish from generalised retinal dystrophies
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the macula
Fundus autofluorescence highlighting hyperautofluorescent vitelliform material
Fluorescein angiography if choroidal neovascularisation is suspected
Molecular genetic testing for BEST1 mutations and family screening
redFlags: Sudden drop in central vision or metamorphopsia suggesting choroidal neovascularisation
New subretinal haemorrhage or fluid at the macula
Rapid progression to atrophy or fibrotic scarring with central scotoma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, with many patients retaining good central vision into later life; however, the fellow eye is usually affected and vision can decline significantly if atrophy, scarring, or choroidal neovascularisation develops.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the vitelliform lesion as age-related macular degeneration and missing the genetic diagnosis
Relying on a normal electroretinogram to exclude the condition when the diagnostic test is the electro-oculogram
Overlooking choroidal neovascularisation as a treatable cause of acute visual loss
Failing to screen at-risk family members given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
